Before you blame the ad, check what happens after the click. When customer acquisition costs rise, it’s tempting to ask for new creative. But a sold-out product, an expired offer, or a checkout issue could be part of the problem. Here’s a review you can run before changing the campaign: 1. Follow the click. Open your ad on your phone. Is the product in stock? Does the offer match what the ad promises? Can you finish checkout? Write down anything that needs attention. Better yet, ask Moby to investigate this for you. And Moby will also document its discoveries for you - so you can still ask what changed, and why. 2. Ask Moby what changed. @triplewhale's AI operator, Moby, can help with the data side of that review. Add your target acquisition cost and any recent changes to promotions or stock, then ask: “Compare the last 7 completed days with the previous 7. Show ad spend, new-customer orders, acquisition cost, and site conversion where available. Keep metric definitions and attribution settings consistent. Flag the biggest changes, show the evidence, and recommend what to check next. Say what you can’t verify.” 3. Review the evidence, then make it recurring. Check how many orders sit behind the change. Make sure the comparison makes sense. Add any context that would be helpful for Moby to know. For supported actions (these actions are based on the recommendations you asked it for), choose “Ask every time” so you can review proposed changes before they run. Once you’re happy with the review, use Moby Automations to run it each week. That’s a useful habit to build before Black Friday: check the buying experience, compare the numbers, and decide what actually needs to change. Before the Black Friday rush, know what needs your attention. Build and own your evals, folks. Why do I keep persisting in this? I do think more and more companies will be forced to operate like a neolab. In other words, more companies will need to own and build their own intelligence stack. This is already happening across many domains. As post-training becomes more accessible, I expect the numbers to accelerate. Access to compute will be a real challenge, but the industry always figures things out. But I think the real moat is in developing evals. I've been working in this space for over a decade, and one thing never changes: what can be properly measured can be more easily optimized. That is crucial in a world of RSI. No software factory without an eval factory. In a world where anyone can build anything, taste matters more. That is codified in evals and further codified in the intelligence stack. I have been building around this in the past year. If you want to chat about this, let's connect.

I like how agents have lowered the bar for building incredible software. As frontier models' capabilities improve, they will subsume more of what traditional software does. In turn, making it easier for more people to build complex software. It's mind-blowing how far you can push a simple custom agent harness and memory system (SQLite/files). Contrary to how people are told to use agents today, I use them to reduce software bloat. I mean, it's crazy how easy it is to build an Instinct-level personal agent with simple primitives. Along the way, we will invent newer primitives that will continue to make it easier to build things. It's an incredible time to be building your own things. You don't have to wait any more for someone to build things for you. Just ask your agent.

Banger report from Google DeepMind. This is also a good example of the type of ambitious work you can now do with frontier models. (bookmark it) They used AI agents to prove key security properties of Signal's code, down to the compiled machine code. Agents powered by Gemini 4 Carbon wrote about 6.5 million lines of Lean proofs on the unmodified libsignal code. A team of five finished the proof work in four weeks. Verifying the seL4 microkernel took twenty person-years. In this work, humans and agents write the security specs, prover agents write the proofs, and Lean checks every proof before it is accepted. When they reintroduced two old Signal bugs, the system proved the buggy versions were insecure. Paper: https://deepmind.google/documents/36/Formal_Verification_of_Signal_4.pdf

Highly recommended read. This is a topic I have been researching and writing about recently. The way we use agent memory in harnesses today works, but mostly for simple, one-off, and general tasks. For more novel, complex, and domain-specific tasks, you will often find that current harness and memory systems don't generalize so well. So the big question is: how can we encode continual learning capabilities in models and harnesses? This is where the idea of co-evolving harnesses and models begins to make sense. This work, along with the benchmark (Continual-ARC), provides an interesting analysis of this. The harness is not just for steering the model and providing tools and context; it is increasingly becoming a key part of training pipelines to unlock continual learning in models. The harness continues to be important, but it can remain minimal and efficient. OpenClaw, Hermes Agent and Prime Agent don't meaningfully learn from experience. On Continual-ARC, our new benchmark at @letsunifyai, none of them were able to memorize anything of value and none were able to generalize to new tasks. Training a small 9B model's weights did both.

A dictation benchmark should help someone choose a tool, not require them to become a speech researcher first. The useful starting question is what they need the tool to write. For a coding workflow, exact technical terms matter. For messages and emails, preserving the intended meaning through restarts and corrections matters. A product can produce fluent text and still fail the task if it changes the detail the user needed to communicate. @voicearena_ai's Dictation Bench is organized around seven use-case categories rather than one generic passage. It also separates the frequency of drafts needing a correction from the total volume of character edits, and shows examples that make those differences understandable. If I were choosing a tool, I would use that evidence to build a shortlist, then test it on my own speech. Latency, privacy, and workflow fit would still matter, but I would start with a clearer picture of output quality. That is the practical significance of a thorough evaluation: it makes a real decision less dependent on a polished demo. The research matters because it helps answer a question people already need to resolve. Drop 4/15: Announcing the Voice Arena Dictation Bench - the first open benchmark of AI dictation apps. Not their APIs: the real apps. We played 761 recordings from 87 speakers into each of 10 apps on a Mac, then 5 LLM judges asked if each draft could be sent as-is. Wispr Flow: 7…

Interesting insights about agent memory. Might be worth a read if you are building memory systems for your agents. Can an agent's memory make it fail tasks it would solve without memory? KAIST researchers find that it can, and they call it memory-induced degradation. The cause is how lessons are stored. They infer lessons from runs labeled only as success or failure, then save them without the run itself. When a lesson is wrong, the agent has no way to verify it. The authors introduce WikiTrace, which stores each lesson as a short insight linked to a summary of why the run succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory. When an insight is vague, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed run, the agent follows the links with terminal tools before acting. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, PlanCraft, AppWorld, and tau3-bench retail, it scores 10.7 points above the agent without memory on average and 3.2 points above the same insights alone. The failure rate for previously solvable tasks drops from 6.5% to 4.5%. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14320 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/dont-just-trust-your-memory-evidence-linked-memory-reduces-memory-induced-degrad-2611.14320

“Software is gonna be so fucking back.” .@CompleteSkeptic is full of bangers and you will have to listen to his full talk at @aiDotEngineer, but for now, here is our top-10 of his pearls: 1“We’ve been announcing AGI three months away for two years now.” Meanwhile, go outside San Francisco and a lot of the world looks unchanged. Where the fuck is all the automation? 2“You get Einstein 95% of the time, but Mr. Bean 5% of the time.” And if you can’t tell which is which, how are you supposed to automate anything? 3“I do believe RLHF is part of the problem.” His complaint: we optimized models for assistance, with a human checking the result, and then expected them to reliably do work on their own. 4“The bitterest lesson is doing the right task.” Diogo thinks that compute matters more than algorithms, data matters more than compute, and choosing the right task matters most. You get what you optimize for. 5“I think the world still has LLM Stockholm Syndrome.” We keep designing around the limitations of today’s models. Why is the best we can come up with still the same software, cheaper to write, with a chatbot on the side? 6“What if we can program with common sense, with intention, with human understanding?” Very passionate talk! He suggests: put intelligence into the software’s inner loop. What could we build if understanding intent became a building block we could actually rely on? 7“Real fucking engineering by people who care a lot about the end result.” Break tasks down, build stages you can verify, and actually manage state. Why should every agent rediscover the same codebase patterns over and over? 8“There’s an asymmetric advantage for people who are, like, bad actors and don’t give a shit.” That’s his explanation for slop: unreliable output is much easier to tolerate when everyone else pays the cost of reading, checking, and filtering it. 9“I call this software research. That’s not a joke.” Explore what software could become, including weird things with no obvious business case. Build something because you can. Maybe one percent of those ideas leads to something awesome. There is going to be SaaSopalooza! (I don’t know how to write this word but you got me) 10“Software is gonna be so fucking back.” The future he wants is one where “can we automate this?” becomes “how much work will it take?”
